strengths: WildFeedback addresses an important NLP problem: learning from naturally occurring user feedback. The pipeline produces 20,281 expert-generated preference pairs and several model-specific variants from real multi-turn conversations.

The GPT-4-data models improve across three established benchmarks, providing evidence of useful training data beyond the proposed evaluation metric. AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rates increase from 17.1% to 31.4% for Mistral and from 22.9% to 34.2% for LLaMA 3.

The human audit of 50 conversations provides partial validation of feedback detection. Reporting precision, recall, and both human–human and model–human agreement is valuable; DSAT precision reaches 83.3%.

The framework is clearly organized, with annotation and evaluation prompts, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters supplied. The reported separation of training and test users and conversations is an appropriate safeguard.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o extracts preferences, generates expert responses, and judges the WildFeedback evaluation; on-policy pairs are also filtered using preference alignment. Figure 2 establishes sensitivity to generated checklists, but does not establish their fidelity to users. The human study validates SAT/DSAT classification only, leaving preference summaries, pairwise labels, and the proposed evaluator unvalidated against human judgments grounded in the original feedback.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. Comparisons are against the original instruction-tuned checkpoints, without matched GPT-4-generated data that omits feedback, an SFT-only ablation, or training on an established preference dataset. Consequently, gains could arise from additional training and teacher distillation. Comparing expert and on-policy variants also changes dataset size, filtering, and response sources simultaneously.

Claims about representative, diverse human preferences exceed the evidence. Feedback-bearing conversations comprise only about 12.8% of the source conversations, and DSAT recall is 48.4%. The test set deliberately selects similar preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training data. This supports evaluation on selected common cases, but does not establish population representativeness or broad preference coverage. The acknowledged selection bias should constrain the abstract and conclusions.

The claim that neither data variant compromises other benchmark performance is contradicted by Table 3. On-policy Mistral drops from 17.1% to 12.9% on AlpacaEval 2 LC, 12.6% to 10.3% on Arena-Hard, and 6.71 to 6.42 on MT-Bench; it also loses more often than it wins without the checklist. Confidence intervals and repeated-run results are absent, limiting interpretation of smaller improvements.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. The manuscript promises future dataset availability but provides no release or implementation link. Exact splits, clustering embeddings, filtering details, generation settings, and the validation protocol for hyperparameter selection are insufficiently specified. Together with the missing independent preference validation and controlled comparisons, these gaps require substantive revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
